title: The US Will Let 20,000 H-1B Holders Renew Visas Without Leaving the Country
excerpt: A December pilot program will spare Indian tech professionals the trip back to a consulate abroad. The vast majority of beneficiaries will be Indian nationals.
body:
For hundreds of thousands of Indian tech professionals living in the United States, renewing an H-1B visa has long meant one thing: booking a flight back to India, waiting weeks for a consular appointment, and hoping that nothing goes wrong with paperwork that could strand them thousands of miles from their homes, their jobs, and their children's schools.

That ordeal is about to change.

The U.S. State Department has confirmed that it will launch a pilot program in December to allow H-1B visa holders to renew their visas without leaving the country. In the first tranche, 20,000 visas will be issued domestically over three months — and the vast majority of those, officials say, will go to Indian nationals.

## 'India Will Benefit Quite a Bit'

Julie Stufft, the Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Visa Services, described the program as a direct response to India-specific backlogs.

"In India, the demand for US visas is still very high. The wait time of 6, 8, and 12 months is not what we need and is not indicative of how we view India," she said. "We are piloting the domestic visa renewal program, which is focused very much on India."

The plan was highlighted during Prime Minister Modi's address to the Indian diaspora at the Ronald Reagan Centre in Washington. It also featured in the joint statement issued by the two governments during Modi's recent visit.

"Because Indians are the largest skilled group of workers in the United States, we hope that India will benefit quite a bit from this program," Stufft said. "It will prevent people from having to travel back to India or anywhere for a visa appointment to get their visa renewed."

## How It Works

Under the pilot, eligible H-1B holders currently living in the U.S. will be able to apply for visa renewal through an online portal, pay the standard processing fee, and mail their passport for stamping — all without setting foot in a consulate abroad. A federal register notice is expected within weeks, laying out eligibility criteria, required documents, and step-by-step instructions for the first cohort.

The State Department had briefly experimented with domestic visa renewal in 2024, processing a limited batch of applications from holders whose previous visas were issued in India or Canada. That pilot was narrow in scope but generated significant demand, filling its allotted slots within days. The December expansion is substantially larger and signals a commitment to making the program permanent.

## What It Means for Indian H-1B Holders

For the estimated 600,000 to 800,000 Indian-born H-1B holders in the United States, the implications are immediate and practical.

Under the current system, an expired visa stamp does not mean loss of legal status — H-1B holders can continue working as long as their I-94 is valid. But a trip outside the U.S. for any reason — a family emergency, a wedding, a parent's illness — requires a valid visa stamp to re-enter. Without domestic renewal, many Indian professionals have avoided international travel entirely for years, effectively trapping themselves within U.S. borders rather than risking the consular appointment lottery.

The domestic renewal option eliminates that trap. It also frees up consular slots in India for first-time applicants, potentially reducing wait times across the board.

## The Bigger Picture

The announcement comes during a complicated moment for Indian professionals in America. A separate bill introduced by Republican Congressman Chip Roy, the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act, proposes ending the H-1B pathway to permanent residency entirely. Another proposed rule threatens to eliminate Day 1 CPT, a lifeline for thousands of Indian graduates. And the Supreme Court is weighing whether birthright citizenship protections apply to children of H-1B holders born on American soil.

Against that backdrop, the domestic renewal pilot is a rare piece of unambiguously good news — a tangible benefit that saves money, time, and anxiety for the community that uses the H-1B program more than any other.

A federal register notice with full eligibility details is expected in the coming weeks. Indian-born H-1B holders should monitor the State Department's consular affairs page for updates.
